summaries.example: Imagine seeing a bright red ball. First, you can simply notice the ball. Brentano says that noticing can already include a basic “yes, this is there.” That is different from thinking, “This ball is red,” which connects the ball with a property. You might also doubt your eyes while still seeing the ball. This shows why seeing, accepting, and describing are related but not exactly the same.
summaries.summary: Franz Brentano studied what happens in the mind when we judge. He separated judgement from presentation. A presentation is simply having something before the mind. A judgement adds acceptance or rejection. For example, seeing a bird may be a presentation, while accepting the bird as really there is a judgement. Brentano argued that this basic acceptance does not need to be a sentence such as “The bird exists.” He also said that a negative judgement and a positive judgement can be directed at the same object: one accepts it and the other rejects it. In his early theory, he tried to explain ordinary forms such as “Some S are P” or “All S are P” by translating them into statements about what exists. Later, he gave up the idea that every judgement has one uniform form. His theory of “double judgements” says that a statement such as “That thing is warm” may first accept the thing and then accept it together with the feature warm. The entry explains both Brentano’s ideas and the reasons they remain difficult and debated.
key_ideas: Brentano says a judgement is not just putting two ideas together.
A presentation can show us something without our deciding whether it is true.
Judging can mean accepting an object or rejecting it, not necessarily saying a full sentence.
He first tried to explain many statements as claims about what exists, but later changed his mind.
His later view says some ordinary judgements are made of more than one judgement.
summaries.why_it_matters: Brentano’s theory asks a basic question: what is the difference between merely thinking of something and accepting or rejecting it? The answer affects how we understand truth, existence, perception, and reasoning. It also shows that ordinary sentences may hide what happens in the mind. Studying his changing view teaches us that philosophical theories can be powerful while still needing revision.

important_terms.definition: A mental act in which someone accepts something or rejects it. Brentano includes some acts of perception among judgements.
A mental act of having or noticing something in thought without yet accepting or rejecting it.
A basic mental “yes” to an object, or a basic “no” to it. Brentano uses this to explain judgement.
A statement or thought that something exists or does not exist.

questions_to_think_about: Can you see something without deciding what it is?
Is noticing a thing the same as saying that it exists?
Why might a philosopher want one explanation for many kinds of judgement?
Can someone see something but not trust that it is real?

summaries.example: Suppose you see a yellow canary but have been told that you may be hallucinating. Brentano distinguishes the presentation of the canary from judging it to be real. In his view, perception can itself involve a simple acknowledgement of an object, without predicating a property of it. Your later judgement that there is no real bird in the scene may conflict with that first acknowledgement. This example illustrates both his non-predicative account of judgement and the possibility that opposing mental acts can coexist, although only one can be correct.
summaries.summary: Brentano’s theory begins with a broad conception of intentionality: mental acts are directed toward objects. Judgement is one basic kind of intentional act, but it is not reducible to presentation. A presentation supplies an object to consciousness; judgement adds acknowledgement or rejection. Brentano therefore denies that judging essentially consists in combining a subject-concept and a predicate-concept. His argument from perception claims that perception is judgement although it need not predicate anything. On this view, an existential judgement acknowledges or rejects an object rather than attaching an existence-property to it. This supports a distinction between the object or content presented and the mode in which it is judged. Brentano also holds that truth concerns the correctness of judgement and need not be explained by positing propositions as objects to which truth is predicated. In his early theory, categorical forms—universal and particular statements—are reduced to existential forms. For instance, “All S are P” is analyzed through the nonexistence of an S that is not P, while “Some S are P” is analyzed through the existence of an S that is P. The source notes that this reduction is controversial and depends on assumptions about meaning and subject matter. Brentano later abandons the universal reduction thesis. His theory of double judgements treats some categorical judgements as involving an initial acknowledgement of a subject and a further judgement involving a predicate. This preserves a distinction between predication and judgement while accepting that not all judgements receive one uniform psychological analysis.
key_ideas: Brentano treats judgement as fundamentally different from presentation, not merely as a more vivid presentation or a combination of ideas.
He argues that perception can be a non-predicative judgement: an acknowledgement or rejection of an object.
Truth need not require a proposition that is itself treated as an object with the property of being true; a judgement can be assessed for correctness.
Existential judgements do not, on his account, predicate existence of an object.
The early reduction thesis translates categorical forms into existential forms, but later Brentano rejects the claim that all judgements have one uniform form.
The later theory of double judgements explains some categorical judgements as structured combinations of simpler judgements, while leaving existential judgements distinct.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory connects philosophy of mind with logic, epistemology, and metaphysics. It asks whether truth and existence can be understood through acts of judging rather than through special abstract objects or properties. It also highlights a persistent issue in philosophy: the grammatical form of a sentence may not reveal the structure of the mental act it expresses. Brentano’s shift from reduction to double judgements shows how pressure from perception, negation, and logical form can force a theory to become less uniform but more nuanced.

important_terms.definition: For Brentano, an intentional mental act that acknowledges or rejects an object; in his broad usage, some perceptions count as judgements.
A mental act directed toward an object without thereby accepting or rejecting it.
A basic mode of mentally taking an object as accepted or rejected, rather than predicating a property of a subject.
A judgement concerning whether something exists or does not exist, understood by Brentano without treating existence as an ordinary property.
The view in Brentano’s early theory that categorical forms can be translated into existential forms without a change in meaning.
Brentano’s later account in which a seemingly single judgement can contain an initial acknowledgement and a further acknowledgement involving a predicate.
Attributing a property to a subject, as in saying that an object is red. Brentano distinguishes this from judging itself.

questions_to_think_about: If perception is a judgement, what could count as its opposite?
Does acknowledging an object require possessing the concept of existence?
Can translating a sentence preserve its meaning while changing the kind of judgement it expresses?
Does the double-judgement theory clarify ordinary statements, or make them unnecessarily complex?
Can a logical reform succeed even if the psychological theory supporting it is rejected?

summaries.example: Imagine looking at a strange shape through a window. You notice it, but you are unsure whether it is a real cat or a reflection. Brentano would separate the presentation—the shape as it appears—from judgement. If you acknowledge the cat, you accept the object as there. If you reject it, you deny it. These acts can concern the same object even though they point in opposite directions. The example also shows why simply combining the ideas “cat” and “reflection” does not by itself amount to a judgement.
summaries.summary: Franz Brentano’s theory of judgement examines how the mind accepts, rejects, and thinks about objects. He distinguishes a presentation, in which something is before the mind, from a judgement, in which the object is acknowledged or rejected. This difference is not merely a difference in strength or vividness, and it does not require combining two ideas. Brentano’s broad use of “judgement” includes perception: seeing a color, sound, or object can involve acknowledging it as present, even without saying that it has a particular property. He also argues that existential judgements do not work by adding the property “existence” to an object. Instead, they acknowledge or reject the object itself. This helps explain how positive and negative judgements can be directed toward the same content. Brentano’s early reduction thesis says that categorical forms can be rewritten as existential ones. “All S are P,” for example, is treated as saying that no S lacking P exists; “Some S are P” is treated as saying that an S that is P exists. He uses this idea to challenge parts of traditional logic. However, the source notes that the reduction depends on controversial assumptions and is not needed for every logical reform. In later work, Brentano gives up the claim that every judgement is existential. His double-judgement theory says that a sentence such as “The rose is a flower” may involve first acknowledging the rose and then making a further acknowledgement that includes the predicate. Thus, his mature view accepts different kinds and levels of judgement rather than forcing them all into one pattern.
key_ideas: Brentano distinguishes the act of presenting an object from the act of judging it.
A judgement is not simply a vivid presentation or a combination of two ideas.
He argues that perception may involve a basic acknowledgement without a subject-predicate statement.
Positive and negative judgements may share the same object or presented content while differing in how the mind relates to it.
In his early theory, categorical statements are reduced to existential statements.
Later, Brentano rejects a fully uniform theory and develops the idea of double judgements.
summaries.why_it_matters: Brentano’s ideas help us examine the gap between language and thought. A sentence may look like a simple subject-predicate statement even when the mental activity behind it is more complicated. His account also links everyday perception with questions about truth, existence, and logic. The later revision is important because it shows philosophical reasoning in action: a theory may preserve central insights while abandoning a claim that no longer seems convincing.

important_terms.definition: A mental act of accepting or rejecting something; Brentano uses the term broadly enough to include certain perceptions.
Having something in mind or before consciousness without yet accepting or rejecting it.
Accepting an object as a basic mental “yes,” without necessarily describing it with a predicate.
A judgement that says something exists or does not exist.
The claim that categorical statements can be analyzed as existential statements about what does or does not exist.
A later account in which one apparent judgement contains an initial acknowledgement and a further judgement involving a property.

questions_to_think_about: What extra mental act turns a presentation into a judgement?
Can a person see something while refusing to accept that it is real?
Why does Brentano think “exists” should not work like an ordinary adjective?
What is gained, and what might be lost, by translating “All S are P” into an existential form?
Does the later theory solve the problems of the earlier one?
